items.text: SF's favorite ice cream sandwich just made a big change
items.article: The mint flavor of San Francisco's favorite It's-It ice cream cookie sandwiches has changed color. A major change has come for San Francisco’s beloved It’s-It ice cream sandwiches. The mint flavor of the ice cream cookie sandwich , once an ostentatiously loud shade of green, has changed color, as first spotted by the San Francisco Chronicle. (The Chronicle and SFGATE are both owned by Hearst but have separate newsrooms.) An SFGATE editor bought a box at Andronico’s and confirmed the breaking news — the bright, toothpaste-green ice cream had been drained of color, with a far more muted, pale pastel green in its place. Where the shade once screamed “GREEN!” at the top of its lungs, now, it only whispered. Curiously, though, It’s-It has mostly kept the change quiet. Despite SFGATE’s repeated attempts this week to reach the Burlingame-based company for comment, It’s-It never got back to us. The company has not released any statement announcing the change to its customers, and photos of the mint ice cream sandwich on its website remain the same , advertising the old seafoam green color instead of the new, lighter shade. It’s-It President Charles Shamieh did speak with the Chronicle, telling the outlet that It’s-It made the change due to U.S. Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. items.article: Smit Machchhar says in video call with Indian PM that he realised if he did not get up ‘passengers would lose their lives’ The Indian pilot who helped thwart an apparent attempt to crash a flydubai flight to Tel Aviv said his faith and his desire to save his passengers allowed him to make a “last push” to open the cockpit door as he fought for his life. Capt Smit Machchhar, who was recovering in an Abu Dhabi hospital, described to India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, how he helped save the plane and its more than 170 passengers. “I had suffered so many injuries that I had collapsed. At that time, I could feel that the aircraft was going down. I knew this was the last push,” Machchhar told Modi in a video call on Friday. “I was fighting for my life. At one point, I realised that if I didn’t get up … then passengers would lose their lives.” His Omani co-pilot apparently stabbed him and set the plane on a steep descent, with the aircraft plummeting about 17,000 feet in the span of a minute. While still being attacked, Machchhar managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers to enter, subdue the attacker and ultimately stabilise the plane. The full circumstances of the attack are still under investigation, but a relief crew on the flight helped land the plane safely in Tabouk, north-west Saudi Arabia . items.key: ai:why thousands of couples are choosing scotland to say 'i do'
items.text: Why thousands of couples are choosing Scotland to say 'I do'
items.article: A quarter of all marriages in Scotland involve couples who don't live here but see it as the ultimate wedding destination. Hayden and Savannah had never set foot in Scotland before they decided it was the perfect place to get married last May. The couple, from Pennsylvania in the USA, wanted a destination wedding that would take their family and friends on an adventure with them. They considered locations across Europe, before deciding on Scotland after Savannah saw photographs of a castle wedding online. "I think it was on Pinterest," she said. "Somebody got married in a castle and I was like, 'Oh, I have to do that'." The pair are far from alone in seeing Scotland as the ultimate romantic destination. Nearly a quarter of all marriages registered in Scotland last year involved couples who did not live in the country.
